Samsung says AI to drive technology demand in second half
"In the second half of 2024, business conditions are expected to remain positive with demand - mainly around generative AI - holding strong, despite continued volatility relating to macroeconomic trends and geopolitical issues," Samsung said in a statement.
By Joyce Lee and Heekyong Yang
SEOUL: Samsung Electronics said on Tuesday it expected demand for artificial intelligence to hold strong in the second half, driving sales of memory chips and tech devices, as it reported a more than 10-fold rise in first-quarter operating profit.
The South Korean company's memory chip sales nearly doubled in the first quarter from a year earlier as prices rose steeply from a severe downturn, thanks to the boom in AI.
"In the second half of 2024, business conditions are expected to remain positive with demand - mainly around generative AI - holding strong, despite continued volatility relating to macroeconomic trends and geopolitical issues," Samsung said in a statement.
Samsung shares were up 1.6% in morning trade, outpacing a 0.5% rise in South Korea's benchmark index.
The world's biggest maker of memory chips and TVs said operating profit rose to 6.6 trillion won ($4.8 billion) in January-March, up from 640 billion won a year earlier.
That was in line with Samsung's own estimate of 6.6 trillion won flagged earlier this month, its highest operating profit since the third quarter of 2022.
First-quarter revenue rose 13% to 71.9 trillion won, the company said, including a 96% increase in memory chip revenue to 17.49 trillion won.
It cemented a recovery from an unprecedented memory chip downturn caused by weak post-pandemic demand for gadgets that use chips.
MEMORY CHIP PROFIT
The chip division, historically Samsung's cash cow business that used to make up two-thirds of the company's operating profit, swung to profit of 1.91 trillion won in the March quarter from a 4.58 trillion won loss a year earlier.
Samsung's memory chip business reported a profit for the first time since the third quarter of 2022 due to customers buying chips in anticipation prices would rise further in future.
Prices of NAND flash chips used to store data increased by 23% to 28% during the first quarter versus the previous quarter, while prices of DRAM chips used in tech devices rose by about 20%, according to data provider TrendForce.
South Korean rival SK Hynix said last week it expected a full recovery in the memory chip market on AI demand as it posted its highest profit in nearly two years.
Samsung said it began mass production this month of the latest high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips for use in generative AI chipsets, called 8-layer HBM3E, as it seeks to capitalise on the AI boom that has benefited its rivals.
It said it plans to start making the 12-layer version during the second quarter.
Samsung's mobile devices business booked a 3.51 trillion won operating profit in the first quarter, down from 3.94 trillion won a year earlier. Rising costs, including increased memory chip prices, dented margins from its flagship Galaxy S24 smartphones launched during the quarter.

title: Samsung Profit Soars Tenfold As Chip Demand Rebounds Amid AI Boom
text:
Topline
Samsung Electronics reported a 933% annual increase in first-quarter operating profits, fueled by chip price recovery from a post-pandemic slump and rising demand for artificial intelligence-driven products—marking a turnaround after six consecutive quarters of profit decline.
Key Facts
Samsung posted $52.2 billion (71.9 trillion Korean won) in first-quarter sales, up 13% year over year, slightly falling under FactSet’s consensus estimates of $51.7 billion.
Operating profit soared by a whopping 933% year over year to $4.8 billion (6.6 trillion Korean won), beating analysts expectations of $4.5 billion and ending a series of declines that started in Q3 2022.
In the first quarter of 2023, the company’s operating profit reached a 14-year low due to a post-pandemic slump in memory chip prices; yet prices have started to rebound as demand for advanced High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) chips—crucial for developing complex artificial intelligence applications—has increased amid the AI boom.
The company announced it will continue to increase HBM chips supply this year to “respond to growing demand for generative AI,” in a statement Tuesday.
Shares rose 1.4% in early Seoul trading, reflecting investors’ optimism about the semiconductor giant’s AI bet.
Key Background
Samsung's semiconductor division rode out a challenging period starting in mid-2022 through 2023, as memory chip prices plummeted due to excess inventories built up during the pandemic to meet high consumer electronics demand. In response to weakened gadget demand amid rising post-Covid inflation, the company made significant cuts to its memory chip production to help normalize prices—which, by the first quarter, had risen by around 20%, according to Trendforce, a market research agency. Another boon was a surge in demand for Samsung’s HBM chips, essential for AI processing, which buoyed the semiconductor giant’s profitability. Last month, Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang said his company is in the process of qualifying Samsung’s new HBM chips for Nvidia’s graphics processing units—which led to a 6% rise in Samsung shares immediately after the announcement. CLSA analyst Sanjeev Rana recently noted that the average selling prices of memory chips are expected to "continue to climb further in 2024," driven by “improving memory demand-supply, falling inventory, strong demand from AI applications and HBM production ramp-up.”
Tangent
Though a surge in profits signals a road to recovery after riding out its lowest annual earnings in 15 years in 2023, Samsung initiated an “emergency mode” this month, mandating a six-day workweek for its executives to tackle imminent challenges. These include a steep depreciation of the Korean won, rising oil prices and political risks from the upcoming U.S. presidential election—factors that could hinder Samsung's strategic ambitions within South Korea’s export-driven semiconductor industry.
Crucial Quote
“In the second half of 2024, business conditions are expected to remain positive with demand—mainly around generative AI—holding strong, despite continued volatility relating to macroeconomic trends and geopolitical issues,” Samsung said in the earnings statement Tuesday.
What To Watch For
Whether Samsung's new bet on AI-enabled smartphones and chips will solidify its leadership in both markets. Samsung has reclaimed its position as the largest smartphone maker in Q1—after being dethroned by Apple in 2023—fueled by its newly launched Galaxy S24 series in January. The flagship series, marked by its generative AI features, saw a strong market reception; global sales of S24 grew 8% year over year compared to last year’s Galaxy S23 series during their first three weeks of availability, according to Counterpoint Research. However, “it is too early to expect AI features to drive a strong replacement cycle,” noted Mehdi Hosseini, analyst at Susquehanna, as Chinese manufacturers have also become “more innovative and aggressive” with new 5G smartphone models. The company is also late in the AI memory chip game, where its South Korean competitor SK Hynix has taken an early lead as the primary supplier to Nvidia. Samsung said it plans to mass produce its next-generation HBM chips in the first half of 2024.

Prices of NAND flash chips used to store data increased by 23% to 28% during the first quarter versus the previous quarter, while prices of DRAM chips used in tech devices rose by about 20%, according to data provider TrendForce.
South Korean rival SK Hynix said last week it expected a full recovery in the memory chip market on AI demand as it posted its highest profit in nearly two years.
Samsung said it began mass production this month of the latest high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips for use in generative AI chipsets, called 8-layer HBM3E, as it seeks to capitalise on the AI boom that has benefited its rivals.
It said it plans to start making the 12-layer version during the second quarter.
Samsung's mobile devices business booked a 3.51 trillion won operating profit in the first quarter, down from 3.94 trillion won a year earlier. Rising costs, including increased memory chip prices, dented margins from its flagship Galaxy S24 smartphones launched during the quarter.

title: Do More With Less: Three AI Programs For Automotive Efficiency
text:
The phrase “Work smarter, not harder” has been the over-recycled phrase of so many executives that some Corporate Bingo cards feature the mantra as the first-overall square. In a moment of honesty, many of those management speeches don’t fully understand how to accomplish said efficiency improvements, but quietly realize it’s their responsibility to solve the “do more with less” conundrum.
However, with the breakthrough changes enabled by several generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) products, automotive executives may have found the solutions to their efficiency gains: Empwr.ai, Humaxa and JACoB.
Empwr.ai
Per a 2023 study by Gartner, 80 to 90% of all new business data is unstructured, and it’s growing three times faster than structured data. “We want to make that data useful,” states Jeremiah Seraphine, the Entreprenuer in Residence in charge of Ewpwr.ai. “Through our partner, UpLevel, we know that 40% of employees’ time is consumed in meetings, but executives don’t know the outcomes. Is this the right amount of time? On the right topics or projects?”
Therein, Empwr.ai has a double-pronged approach at the micro and macro-level. For the individual contributors, it not only records the meetings for later consumption, but it also bolsters his/her effectiveness by producing a weekly digest of Action Items accumulated throughout the meetings. Arguably even more valuable, the executives receive a dashboard providing oversight of the team’s efficiency, confirms those meetings are focused on the highest priorities, and helps with cross-organizational project management.
Interestingly, part of what inspired Empwr.ai’s feature set was Seraphine’s eighteen months as a Chief of Staff at a major automaker. “It’s difficult for executive leadership to pierce mid-management to see what’s actually happening with the rank and file. Frequently, it’s old news for the ground level when executives finally understand that a project is off-track.”
Humaxa
Those who have migrated a product between regions, customers, teams, etc. know the herculean tasks of consuming the relevant standards and requirements, training the distributed team and understanding how these constraints impact your product. Weeks. Months. Some of the standards (e.g., Functional Safety or ISO 26262) are enormous, convoluted and, frankly, ambiguous at times. Sifting through thousands of pages of engineering-speak to formulate your project’s system requirements can create a bottleneck at the beginning of the process, or inject immeasurable risk at the end upon the realization that “my widget” doesn’t meet regulations or requirements.
Huge inefficiencies.
“For example, I just had a conversation with a software developer,” stated the Chief Marketing Officer of Humaxa, Jennifer Gargulinski, “and 90% of his time is spent reading documentation, specifications, standards, regulations, etc. so that only 10% of his time is left for actual coding.” Humaxa then demonstrated the power of AI with this coder using connectivity and cybersecurity standards and proved that time spent on a new task was reduced from an estimated sixteen (16) hours to one (1) hour (i.e., 94% efficiency improvement). “Standards are not written with nice summaries or easy-to-find portions, so what typically happens for practical purposes: the document must be read from beginning to end and then maybe annotated.”
Gargulinski believes AI will enhance existing jobs. “Generative AI can be thought of like a calculator of words. Calculators are used for millions of existing jobs to analyze numbers. We are just at the very beginning of AI. It’s going to be a very exciting road.”
JACoB
Ironic: code begets code. In some ways, it’s surreal. In other ways, it’s a fascinating efficiency worth considering.
“I've been using AI for coding for the past three years or so, but it wasn't until I got access to GPT-4 last March that I really started to explore how far I could push the AI to help me to build real working code,” relates Kevin Leneway, a Principal Software Engineer at PSL and the Project Maintainer of JACoB (Just Another Coding Bot). “I’ve found that with the right prompts and context from my code base, GPT-4 can efficiently handle the mundane parts, allowing me to focus on the higher-level planning and complex coding tasks to get the whole project up and running. It reinvigorated my joy of coding in a way that I haven’t felt since I was a kid tinkering with my Commodore 64.”
In fact, a 2023 study found that developers using generative AI tools experienced a productivity surge of up to 50% for tasks such as code documentation and generation, with lesser improvements for code refactoring (20-30%) and highly-complex work (<10%).
“As we're already seeing with coding agents,” states Leneway, “even today's limited AI models are changing the way software is written and these changes are only going to accelerate over time.”
Author’s Note
Will auto-generated code, standards demystification or meeting oversight replace the software architects and project managers of yesteryear? Certainly not. But per the 2023 Forbes article “Artificial Intelligence: Why Auto Companies Are Redesigning Cars and Suppliers” and the Mark Cuban video above, many jobs shall be reshaped. “AI will unleash a new level of productivity and innovation,” predicted Ludovic Hauduc, CTO of Envorso and former VP of Engineering for Meta (in charge of their AI infrastructure). “Just like a large percentage of jobs from the 1950’s no longer exist today, it’s likely that 30% of all current jobs will be reshaped somehow in the next 2-3 years through automation. The speed of innovation around AI is unlike any technological shift we’ve seen before.”
So the executives who want to work smarter (rather than harder), might want that extra intelligence.

title: TikTok And Instagram Have An AI Influencer Problem. Blockchain Can Help.
text:
The rise of truly powerful and accessible, Generative AI (GenAI) is beginning to shake up the social media landscape. New AI tools and even influencers are beginning to shape how we interact through platforms like TikTok and Instagram. This is not only troubling in terms of what content can be generated or spread but is also an existential threat to human creators as well. The solution to this problem lies in what blockchain technology can offer in terms of verified, human digital identities.
The Rise Of The AI Influencer
Just recently, TikTok announced it was testing a new in-app tool to allow users to utilize AI to generate avatar images. The tool will let users submit photos of themselves and create unique images in a range of poses and styles. These can then be downloaded, shared, or used as a custom profile picture.
This straightforward tool can enable anyone to have a visually interesting avatar that they may otherwise not be able to create themselves. Furthermore, it’s free and nearly instantaneous, empowering creativity and lowering the barrier to access. That is a noble idea and solid in theory, but it is also just the beginning. Another recent revelation from TikTok is that the platform is also exploring creating AI-driven influencers who could promote brands, talk about various topics, and generally do exactly what influencers already do — only they wouldn’t be real.
AI influencers aren’t entirely new, with prominent profiles like Imma and Shudu attracting hundreds of thousands of followers. However, until very recently digitally created influencers cost more than a real human being to deploy. That’s changing fast. Tools like ChatGPT, Midjourney, and many others are making it affordable for anyone to create high-quality content with just a few sentences, and there’s no reason to think this trend will slow down.
Soon, it isn’t going to be just big brand names who may create their own AI influencers; it will be anyone. Once built, they can then use these personas to promote anything they want. Think about what fake accounts and bots are already doing to social media and it shouldn’t be hard to imagine how dangerous this could be.
In the words of Ed Keller, a leading authority on word of mouth and influencers, and author of the Influentials, “At the core of word of mouth’s power, including word of mouth from creators, is trust. That’s what makes it so powerful and is fueling its growth. The influence of unchecked, unverified AI is troubling, and shows how quickly new technology might destroy trust in the online world. This is bad news for everyone who uses the internet, and particularly for real-life influencers because they have such a big digital footprint that can be used to train hyper-realistic, ultra-believable clones of themselves. There are potential negative consequences for marketers as well, if the rise of fake creators undermines the very foundation that has led to the huge rise in the size and credibility of the creator economy.”
The threat of bad faith actors spreading misinformation and hateful content, influencing public opinion, and even potentially shaping the course of politics is too real to be ignored. At this point, there is no putting the genie back in the bottle. As OpenAI made clear in a recent statement addressing criticism from Elon Musk: “We’re making our technology broadly usable in ways that empower people and improve their daily lives, including via open-source contributions. We provide broad access to today's most powerful AI, including a free version that hundreds of millions of people use every day.”
Even if a given government tried to combat this new online reality, by creating rules around what type of AI content can be created and spread, they wouldn’t be universally applied. Additionally, some people will always be willing to break the law, so while solid regulations should be put in place, this problem is bigger than what the legal world alone can tackle.
How Blockchain Technology & Digital Identities Can Save Us From The Machines
We have to accept that there’s no going back, while also designing a practical solution for moving forward. This is where blockchain can support us. Instead of controlling what is allowed to be generated, a system can be created to identify the content's original source. Whether it be a human or an AI, consumers will be able to see where it came from and make informed decisions about how they interact with it.
This is especially important given the importance social media has on society. Marketing strategist and best selling author Mark Schaefer believes we’re on the cusp of a profound moment in business. “From now, on, the number one question our customers will have is, ‘Is this real?’ Businesses must spare no expense protecting their brand, executives, and employees from deep fakes. I think blockchain has to play a role in this as a source of truth.
“I’m concerned that businesses have no idea what’s coming,” Schaefer said. “A brand is trust. No trust, no brand. That should worry everyone.”
Recently, leaders in Davos were thinking about how blockchain can be used to track, sort, and manage the data that AIs are being trained on. As Sheila Warren, the CEO of the Crypto Council for Innovation, stated to CNBC: “I actually do think that the verification of an AI and sort of the checks and balances ...are going to be blockchain driven and blockchain-backed.” This is a good start for building trustworthy autonomous identities, but what about untrustworthy ones?
Decentralized technology can provide credentials in a fully verifiable and unfalsifiable way, due to the immutability and transparency of these networks. Blockchains cannot realistically be hacked or manipulated, and any changes made to them are always able to be seen by all participants.
If we want digital profiles that come with verifying credentials, this technology is the way to go. With this, Digital IDs can be provided to every human and artificial participant on social media, defining their online persona, history, preferences, and any other information they choose to share. In the interest of privacy, much of this data would be self-encrypted and under the control of the users, who could decide what is and isn’t for the public to see. However, one parameter that should always remain public is their proof of humanity or lack thereof.
Real people can perform a “humanity check,” to prove they are real, and human influencers can additionally link a wide array of credentials to make it clear they are who they say. However, any AI influencers would also need to be transparent about that fact, in a way that cannot be circumvented.
In such a system, any profile that doesn’t have the humanity credential could be assumed to be machine-generated. This doesn’t mean this content is nefarious, but it would give consumers a degree of awareness of what they are taking in. Social media platforms would be free to tag, block, or filter AI content in any way they saw fit, but gone would be the days where bots could influence the social discourse without oversight.
This isn’t like the “blue check” on X, where users pay a fee and get an icon next to their name and that’s about it. This would be available exclusively through the user providing some form of meaningful proof of who they are, probably confirmed by another verified human, and only then would their blockchain-enforced credential be awarded. With this, users could trust that a verified account is exactly that, and not just someone who was able to pay the entrance fee.
Concluding Thoughts on AI Avatars
If built correctly, such a system could allow us to navigate this brave new world of AI in a way that retains individual privacy, the freedom to choose human sources, and the ability for people to make a living via content creation. Along the way, there will be many details to navigate, but there is currently no other plausible model for protecting social media from the growing impacts of AI. Laws can only go so far, we need something practical to put in place.
Blockchain and digital identities provide a realistic means to protect consumers and the human workforce. This is a step we need to take soon because the speed of AI development isn’t slowing down. However, there is an opportunity for a more powerful and safer internet for the next generation and beyond.

title: Council Post: Human Ingenuity And AI: Working Together For Amazing Results
text:
Every day, we hear more and more about what artificial intelligence can do. AI tools (including generative AI) are taking over tasks that have traditionally been done by humans. Still, no matter its ongoing evolution, AI is simply a tool, and its biggest—and most positive—impacts come when it’s used to support the inherent talents and ingenuity of human beings.
Combining the capabilities of AI with the oversight and creativity of human users and operators can not only achieve better business processes, but also deliver outcomes that improve our health, protect our environment and enhance our lives. Below, 16 members of Forbes Technology Council share ways human ingenuity and AI are coming together to produce amazing results.
1. Gathering And Reviewing Patient-Focused Information
In healthcare, physicians constantly juggle multiple tasks in a short amount of time. AI can step in to alleviate some of that strain by helping set a gold standard of care and providing relevant, patient-focused information. But at the end of the day, doctors still need to form treatment plans themselves and apply clinical judgment to the information they gather from AI. - Michal Tzuchman Katz MD, Kahun Medical
2. Bringing Clarity And Focus To Meetings
People waste a lot of time in meetings, which is expensive when you consider payroll costs and lost productivity. But there’s a way to make meetings more efficient and effective with technology. AI and GenAI can handle low-value activities such as scheduling, creating agendas, taking notes and sharing content. This enables people to focus on high-value collaborative work activities. - Alfredo Ramirez, Vyopta

3. Testing Software Solutions
I see a good opportunity to improve the quality and testing of software and business workflows. AI can be trained to understand your intentions for a product and verify how well your technical solution achieves those intentions. This speeds time to value, profitability and customer success. - Agur Jõgi, Pipedrive
4. Responding To Localized Disasters
In disaster response situations, AI and drones can quickly map devastated areas, identifying hazards and survivors. Human teams can then use this data to efficiently plan rescues, deliver aid and manage logistics, greatly improving response times and outcomes in the critical first hours. - Margarita Simonova, ILoveMyQA
5. Protecting Against Cybersecurity Threats
As security operations centers are hit by advancing attack tactics, budget cuts and the widening cyber skills gap, AI can help SOC analysts regain productivity and focus on their most complex threat remediation tasks. By identifying patterns and anomalies in email and software as a service environments, for example, AI can support the detection of email compromises, account takeovers or risky configuration drifts. - Mike Britton, Abnormal Security
6. Optimizing Power Generation And Distribution
In the energy sector, AI and generative AI can collaborate with human experts to optimize power generation and distribution. AI can analyze real-time data from smart grids and renewable energy sources to predict demand fluctuations and adjust supply accordingly. Human engineers can use AI-generated insights to make strategic decisions about infrastructure investments and maintenance. - Marc Fischer, Dogtown Media LLC
7. Providing Fast, Personalized Customer Service
One significant case is customer service. AI can be used to handle initial customer interactions, answering common questions using data-driven insights. Generative AI can take this a step further by creating customized responses, making the interaction more personal. Humans can step in for challenging issues, providing the personal touch and critical thinking that AI currently struggles to replicate. - Robert Mao, ArcBlock Inc.
8. Generating Marketing Content
AI and human collaboration excel in creative content generation for marketing purposes. AI analyzes data for initial ideas, and humans refine and personalize outputs, leading to innovative, effective campaigns. - Favour Femi-Oyewole, Access Bank PLC
9. Detecting Financial Fraud
In financial services, AI and generative AI can analyze transaction data to detect fraud, while human expertise applies nuanced judgment for investigation. This collaboration boosts detection accuracy, speeds response and reduces false positives, enhancing asset protection and customer trust in a rapidly evolving financial landscape. - Imane Adel, Paymob
10. Developing Personalized Educational Content
AI and humans can dramatically improve outcomes in education by personalizing learning experiences for students and making the learning process more enjoyable and interactive. Imagine an app with a multimodal chatbot (chat, image and video) that helps students complete their homework and prepare for tests, recommends practice problems and study materials based on the student’s focus area, and more. - Chet Kapoor, DataStax
11. Detecting Early Signs Of Cancer
In cancer detection, AI and clinicians form a powerful alliance: AI processes and learns from millions of pathology images, spotting early, subtle signs of cancer with superhuman precision. Doctors then interpret these insights, combining their experience and intuition to make accurate diagnoses and tailor treatments, vastly improving early detection rates and patient outcomes. - Nicola Sfondrini, PWC
12. Capturing Expert Knowledge
Companies have vast amounts of expert knowledge that is often held in unstructured data formats, such as text files and PDFs. Capturing this knowledge so it can be shared across the company can be made much easier with generative AI. This is crucial, because expert knowledge provides context and nuance to machine learning findings—in effect, making AI recommendations more applicable. - AJ Abdallat, Beyond Limits
13. Forecasting Product Demand
In supply chain management, AI and generative AI, coupled with human expertise, enhance predictive analytics for demand forecasting. By integrating historical data, market trends and human insights, businesses can streamline inventory management, reduce overstock and meet customer demands with greater accuracy and efficiency, ultimately boosting profitability and customer satisfaction. - Rohit Anabheri, Sakesh Solutions LLC
14. Speeding New Drug Discovery
Traditionally slow and expensive, drug discovery is a prime example of how AI and humans can work together to optimize a process. AI excels at analyzing vast amounts of data, which helps researchers identify potential drug candidates. Generative AI can take it further by designing molecules that could be used in new medicine. Human expertise and precision then guide the search and find the best options. - Thomas Griffin, OptinMonster
15. Managing Risk
Risk management is dependent on input parameters and modeling various scenarios, including edge cases, which are often related to catastrophes (such as the Covid-19 pandemic). While humans are very good at describing boundary conditions, AI is superior in modeling various scenarios, including statistical predictions of catastrophic cases on the edges of models. - Ondrej Krehel
16. Tackling Food Scarcity
In sustainable agriculture, AI and humans partner to tackle food scarcity. AI analyzes climate data and crop genetics to optimize planting strategies, while human farmers apply traditional knowledge and hands-on care. This synergy boosts yield and resilience, addressing hunger with precision and wisdom. - Andrew Blackman, EZ Cloud

title: Council Post: KMS And LLM Integration: Best Practices For A Smooth Transition
text:
CEO of KMS Lighthouse. Leading the company's vision to disrupt the knowledge management market.
There are countless ways to pose a question, each with its nuances and contextual layers. From the straightforward "what is ..." to the open-ended "how can I ..." the queries can be as diverse as the people asking them. However, no matter how they’re asked, they all share a common thread—the desire to gain knowledge that enables informed decision-making or solves a problem.
Many employees have complex questions that require information from multiple resources to answer. The solutions they seek are often found in an organization’s vast knowledge management system (KMS) that contains business data, manuals, frequently asked questions, best practices and more. But finding the “perfect” answer isn’t always a simple task.
Remarkable advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), including ChatGPT, now bring us to an exciting intersection. Knowledge and large language models (LLMs) have come together to transform organizational experiences, empower people to tackle complex tasks more efficiently and make better-informed decisions. With LLMs, users can engage in natural human-like conversations that get them relevant, useful information, guidance and recommendations more quickly and easily.
While potential benefits are significant, getting the most out of integrating a KMS and LLMs requires a thoughtful approach. Here, we explore an integration’s practical aspects, focusing on steps for implementation, methodology, common pitfalls and stresses on businesses.
Breaking Barriers: KMS And LLMs
The integration of a KMS and LLMs is ushering in a new era of organizational experiences, where the wall between knowledge and its applications is quickly tumbling down. No longer are employees confined to navigating through vast data reserves, guessing which question will get them the information they need. LLMs are taking knowledge management to the next level, sifting through the ocean of data and generating relevant information in real time.
Putting LLMs In Knowledge Management Into Practice
Implementing LLMs in knowledge management systems (KMSs) can be a game-changer, but achieving maximum results requires careful planning and execution. If your business is contemplating adopting LLM-powered KMS solutions, avoiding common pitfalls and carrying out a series of established steps can ensure a successful integration.
Steer Clear of LLM Integration Missteps
Potential obstacles to a successful LLMs/KMS integration include an overreliance on the technology, ignoring data privacy concerns and neglecting user training. Despite all their advantages, LLMs do have some limitations in knowledge search. Trained on “unsupervised learning,” they can generate inaccurate responses or what has been termed “hallucinations,” producing coherent and grammatically correct outputs that are nonetheless nonsensical or factually incorrect. While sometimes amusing, these results can be particularly concerning in healthcare and other sectors requiring high levels of accuracy.
Taking a strategic approach to implementation can help mitigate these and other potential hindrances.
Step 1: Assess Current KMS
Evaluate your organization’s knowledge management system’s strengths and weaknesses and identify areas where LLM integration can provide the most value. This helps determine the objectives you hope to achieve with the new system, whether it be improved search capabilities, more accurate information retrieval or enhanced user experience.
Step 2: Choose The Appropriate LLM
Consider which features will ensure the LLM aligns with your KMS capabilities and seamlessly fits into your existing infrastructure. Think about factors like language support, scalability and ease of integration.
Step 3: Data Preparation
To provide the most relevant and accurate responses, LLMs require high-quality, well-organized and up-to-date data. Invest time and resources in ensuring your data’s in top shape before integrating the LLM.
Step 4: Integrating And Testing
Adopting an agile approach to integration allows for flexibility and adjustments based on user feedback and system performance. Collaboration between IT, knowledge management and end users is vital during this step, ensuring the system’s designed with the user in mind.
Step 5: Training
Provide comprehensive training sessions and resources to help team members understand the system’s capabilities and how to get the most out of it. This can be instrumental in increasing user adoption and mitigating the risk of overreliance on the technology.
Step 6: Monitoring
Continuous tracking and system refinement are crucial to optimal performance. To improve the LLM integration’s effectiveness, collect user feedback, analyze system performance and make adjustments as needed. This iterative process also helps businesses keep pace with AI’s and LLM’s rapid and ongoing advancements.
Integrating LLMs into a KMS can be a significant shift for organizations, meaning it requires careful change management. Address potential resistance and ensure clear communication about the integration’s benefits and impact. Additionally, be mindful of the resource allocation needed, as implementing and maintaining LLM integration can be resource-intensive.
By focusing on the right steps, adopting a user-centric design and being aware of the common pitfalls, businesses can successfully implement LLMs in their KMS and unlock the full potential of this transformative technology. While no one can say with certainty just how far LLMs will go in enhancing organizational experiences, it’s safe to say they’ll develop an increasingly greater ability to synthesize complex data into actionable insights and relevant responses, a critical feature in a world where customers demand personalized, immediate service. Stay tuned for what’s sure to be an exciting journey moving forward!

title: Council Post: No-Code AI Solutions Crafting The Future
text:
Sunny Pokala, CEO, Amtex Systems.
Artificial intelligence (AI) has come a long way since its early days of testing over more than a decade, and it has emerged as a powerful force that has the potential to revolutionize a wide range of industries. The growing amounts of money being invested in AI projects serve as proof of this development. Artificial intelligence is still a field distinguished by its technical complexity and specialized nature. No-code AI solutions, on the other hand, present a strong path toward democratizing AI in all this complexity. With a forecast revenue of $49,481 million by 2033 and a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 28.3% from 2023 to 2033, the no-code AI platform industry is expected to grow rapidly. This strong growth pattern highlights these platforms' popularity as strong substitutes for well-established AI techniques. As messengers of cost and accessibility, they portend a sea change in the field of artificial intelligence and are symbolic of its transformational potential.
Why Are No-Code AI Solutions Getting Popular?
The implementation of no-code AI is noteworthy for its significant cost savings, which relieves organizations of the need to hire specialized AI talent. This efficient strategy highlights how AI is becoming more accessible to a wider range of businesses, hence democratizing how it is utilized. Furthermore, no-code AI has democratizing effects by enabling nontechnical stakeholders in organizations to lead the development of custom AI systems that are customized to meet their specific operational needs.
Key Challenges In Implementing No-Code AI Solutions
Putting no-code AI solutions into practice is a complex process that crosses the complex fields of data science and software development. With the promise of task automation, actionable insights and improved decision-making frameworks, the development of AI tools is characterized by a complex range of difficulties. In the scope of this talk, we will discuss the main obstacles that no-code AI solutions have to overcome and how they could affect the undertaking's forward progress.
Adapting To The Evolving AI Field
Considering AI continually evolves and there are always new techniques and innovations to keep up with, it requires constant attention. It is a difficult endeavor for developers to include cutting-edge techniques in their repertory and absorb the most recent study findings. A careful balance between innovation and operational robustness is necessary since this endeavor is made more difficult by the need to maintain the stability and functionality of existing systems.
Allocating Resources
Computational capabilities must be wisely allocated in the field of AI and machine learning, especially with the rise of deep neural networks. Training these models requires a significant amount of memory and processing power, making it a resource-intensive process with financial and time constraints. Moreover, developers must strengthen the underlying infrastructure as the AI tool's reach grows to handle increased workloads without experiencing performance deterioration. This requires careful tuning to guarantee scalability without sacrificing productivity.
Handling Complex Data Management
In the field of AI systems, efficient data management is fundamental. The number, diversity and quality of the underlying data corpus are all closely related to the effectiveness of AI algorithms. Obtaining large amounts of relevant, diverse data while carefully screening it to remove biases and errors is a difficult task for developers. To make the data suitable for consumption by AI models, preprocessing is also required. This is a complex operation because real-world datasets are often unstructured.
Maintaining Ethical Standards
Sustaining ethics in the field of AI research is a complex undertaking that is emphasized by a variety of factors. The protection of privacy, reducing bias and reducing possible technological misuse are the most important of these issues, as they all have concrete consequences in everyday life. Achieving a balance between innovation and problem requires careful navigating of complex legal environments, as well as putting in place strict data governance guidelines and thorough ethics review processes. These steps are vital for developing an accountable culture and making sure AI technology is utilized.
Overcoming The Challenges With No-Code AI-Empowered Solutions
No-code AI tools are user-friendly, even nontechnical people may construct AI-driven solutions with ease. By making AI development more accessible, a wider audience can utilize AI's potential for a range of applications. Businesses can seamlessly integrate AI capabilities into their existing systems by using these platforms' connectivity with a wide range of APIs and data sources. Organizations may optimize their workflows, obtain useful insights and make better decisions by integrating AI-driven insights with their existing applications.
No-code AI platforms prioritize security measures to protect user data and maintain the privacy of sensitive information, in addition to their functional features. These platforms are protected against unwanted breaches by utilizing strong data storage techniques, industry-standard encryption protocols and strict access controls. Furthermore, the platform's integrity and dependability are strengthened by reputable no-code AI providers who conduct regular security assessments and release updates on schedule to address any known issues.
Final Thoughts
The horizon of no-code AI heralds promising prospects, characterized by progressive strides in domains such as natural language processing (NLP), computer vision and reinforcement learning. The synergy between artificial intelligence and no-code methodologies heralds a paradigm shift, empowering citizen developers—individuals lacking formal coding proficiencies—to actively engage in AI development endeavors. This innovative solution for businesses is distinguished by its intuitive, visual interfaces, effectively democratizing AI development and furnishing citizen developers with the means to craft bespoke AI applications tailored to the exigencies of their respective departments.
No-code AI fosters an environment that is favorable to creativity and cooperative synergism by eliminating traditional technological barriers. This inclusive culture accelerates organizational efforts and helps achieve AI-focused goals in addition to increasing the overall effectiveness of diverse teams. Furthermore, improved compatibility with emerging technologies is conceivable, making no-code AI even more adaptable and pervasive in a variety of industrial settings.

title: Council Post: How GovTech Is Shaping The Public Sector And What It Means For Entrepreneurs
text:
Co-Owner at P2H.
Public services are frequently perceived as rigid, cumbersome and difficult to navigate. They often lack speed, user-friendly interfaces and other essential features. This is not merely a subjective matter; governments worldwide have acknowledged the need to enhance the efficiency and inclusivity of their services.
For example, the United Arab Emirates created its Digital Government Strategy 2025, which aims for comprehensive digital integration across government sectors. Furthermore, in 2023, the city of Hamburg, Germany, launched a govtech Campus to digitize its administration and enhance collaboration with innovators and startups through cloud technology.
Being the co-owner of a company that develops platforms for businesses and government agencies, I've seen how digital platforms can provide a wide range of services to citizens and organizations, including automated tax filings, real-time public transportation updates, online voting systems, digital health records access and more. Government platforms can also help to engage communities and, together with them, tackle emerging issues.
Govtech is also a prospective market that's grown in recent years. Here are what I see as the most intriguing technological innovations that can elevate public services to a new level and create an enticing niche for entrepreneurs.
Artificial Intelligence
The latest buzz surrounding AI has not gone unnoticed by governments. In January, the European Commission outlined a strategic vision "to foster the internal development and use of lawful, safe and trustworthy" AI systems in anticipation of implementing the EU AI Act, "the world's first comprehensive law on AI." In the U.S., New Jersey and California governments are exploring potential uses for generative AI in streamlining operations, such as drafting memos or analyzing public feedback on state policies.
A Deloitte report noted that generative AI can play a valuable role in government agencies. It recommended agencies launch more pilot projects to explore generative AI's capabilities and ensure its safe, secure application. AI's potential for policy analysis, summarizing extensive documents or data and generating review-worthy content stands out as key benefits, per the report. I believe anomaly detection represents another valuable area of application, as AI can conduct real-time monitoring to help identify discrepancies, errors or potential fraud.
Smart Cities
Smart Cities, another growing trend, focus on integrating technology, such as the Internet of Things, AI and big data analytics, into urban infrastructure and services. The smart cities market worldwide is projected to have a compound annual growth rate of 12.15% from 2024 and 2028, resulting in a market volume of $165.8 billion in 2028. Through smart technology, cities can optimize everything from traffic and public transport to energy use and waste management. This has the potential to make urban areas more livable, responsive and environmentally friendly.
Several cities around the world have already made strides toward becoming smart cities. One notable example is Singapore's Smart Nation initiative, which supports leveraging data analytics, IoT and AI to improve urban living. Smart Nation focuses on areas such as transport, health and urban solutions. Dubai's smart city project aims to make Dubai the "happiest city on Earth" through smart technology integration in areas such as government services and transportation. Furthermore, for years, Barcelona has used the Internet of Everything to improve parking, lighting and waste management, enhancing energy efficiency and urban planning.
Blockchain
The global blockchain government market was valued at $2.5 billion in 2022 and is expected to exceed $218 billion by 2032. Blockchain technology in govtech offers new ways to enhance transparency, security and efficiency within governments. By enabling decentralized and tamper-proof data storage, blockchain can help streamline processes, reduce fraud and improve trust between government entities and the public. Its potential applications include smart contracts for automated government transactions, identity management solutions and more.
There are several countries around the world that have embraced blockchain technology in govtech. These include the UAE, Australia, Georgia and India. Estonia is another example; it has been at the forefront of integrating blockchain to secure its e-governance ecosystem. A notable example is its KSI Blockchain, which supports various state registries, including business, healthcare, property, digital court and more.
Lessons For Entrepreneurs
To sum up, the demand for govtech is growing, serving to enhance the efficiency, transparency of local governments and citizen engagement. With strategic visions and comprehensive laws guiding the implementation of the Internet of Things, AI and blockchain, these technologies have the potential to reshape administrative operations and urban landscapes, thus paving the way for more sustainable and digitally empowered societies.
As a result, I believe there are possibilities for entrepreneurs to either create new startups with a focus on govtech or expand their businesses by adding new products. However, there are some aspects to bear in mind before entering this market.
Firstly, you have to know not only about technologies but also about regulations of public services. Carefully studying local legislation is one of the keys to success. Secondly, you'll need to secure a government contract to create a govtech product. That can take some time, considering bureaucratic procedures. Finally, geographical scaling can be tricky. Researching the new market, competitors' field, and simply adapting your existing product is not enough. You have to dive into every detail of how public services work in a new region, what rules they follow, etc. That is a time-consuming process that could require significant funding. But do not be scared. Hard work and patience will not let you down.

title: Council Post: A Small Businesses Roadmap For Safe And Secure AI
text:
Grayson Milbourne is a security intelligence director at OpenText Cybersecurity.
Every business, big or small, should consider taking advantage of generative AI to modernize, scale and meet the high demands of customers. Already, according to McKinsley’s State of AI in 2023 report, nearly one-quarter of respondents across the globe are regularly using generative AI in their work.
For small- and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) that have fewer resources but just as much demand, leveraging generative AI can be especially helpful. Generative AI has endless business applications. Tools like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, for example, are already being used to streamline tedious tasks and brainstorm new company initiatives and solutions.
While businesses shouldn’t shy away from using generative AI in operations, it’s important to implement it with security top of mind. By considering generative AI’s cybersecurity risks and creating the necessary safeguards and user guidance, businesses and their security teams can enjoy the benefits of these innovative tools without compromising safety.
Generative AI Benefits For SMBs
AI already offers small businesses across industries many benefits to improve operations. Here are a few to consider.
1. Creating Efficiencies For Manual Tasks: Using AI can reduce the time spent on repetitive tasks while also enabling employees to focus on more strategic and engaging projects. On the security side, AI can improve a business’ knowledge of its data and make it easier to apply proper access controls to reduce risk. This can help IT security teams discover anomalies that can indicate compromise by providing better-prioritized alerts, which support earlier detection, more comprehensive responses and an overall improved security posture.
2. Providing Customer Support: AI-powered chatbots can provide 24/7 support to improve response times and customer satisfaction. Many also have strong built-in security protocols to protect sensitive information. Additionally, AI can analyze customer feedback to identify trends, helping SMBs proactively address common issues and improve overall service.
3. Brainstorming New Solutions And Ideas: AI can help with problem-solving and providing additional ideas to resource-strapped teams. By creating structure, guiding teams through brainstorming processes and reducing groupthink, AI can be a key new tool to generate creative ideas that pull from broad insights and data sets.
Potential Generative AI Pitfalls
While generative AI can fill a gap for SMBs, it also introduces a new attack surface to manage compliance complications and risks of data loss or leakage.
1. Data Privacy Breaches: Employees using AI tools might accidentally access or expose sensitive information, leading to potential data breaches that can cause severe financial and reputational loss.
2. Large Data Requirements: Generative AI requires vast amounts of data to train effectively. This can be challenging for smaller businesses with limited resources. Relying on inadequate or insufficient data could also result in poor performance or biased outcomes.
3. New Attack Vectors: The introduction of generative AI creates new ways for malicious actors to exploit tech stack vulnerabilities, such as manipulating input data to generate false outputs or launching attacks on AI model integrity.
4. Compliance Considerations: AI usage raises several compliance issues around data protection regulations, intellectual property rights and ethical standards. SMBs must remain compliant with regulations to mitigate risks and maintain trust with stakeholders.
Roadmap To Keep Data Protected
To address these concerns, SMBs should consider the following best practices to avoid introducing security risks and maintain compliance with regulations.
• Think critically about data access and barriers. When using AI, think about the sources of information the AI can access. Businesses should create barriers that prevent confidential, proprietary or otherwise sensitive information from being accessed or exposed. For example, SMBs should close off AI access to any financial, tax information, core IP and patent pending information, to name a few examples.
• Create an AI policy to guide use and understanding. In October, the U.S. president established an executive order to regulate the security of AI tools amid the technology’s rapid advancement and adoption. By creating their own internal AI policies, SMBs can ensure the preservation and proper treatment of their data while helping employees navigate generative AI in a safe and informed way. To protect generative AI use from all sides, SMBs should also ensure that the third parties they work with are also exercising safe and responsible AI use.
• Harness a third-party checklist. Security must be considered throughout the entire AI supply chain. SMBs should take care to ensure that any third-party AI components are being deployed safely. AI models often involve the use of various datasets, pre-trained models and external libraries, so understanding the origins and security status of these components enhances overall supply chain security. By implementing an AI Bill of Materials (AIBOMs), practitioners can add another layer of AI security that provides insights into a model’s training history, architecture, data dependencies and more.
Conclusion
AI holds a lot of promise for small businesses, but like any new technology, the potential risks can outweigh the positives. If security is prioritized and the above tips are followed, small businesses can more safely build generative AI use into their operations to reap its benefits while staying protected.

title: Council Post: Beyond The GenAI Hype: Three Considerations For Practical Adoption
text:
R. Srikumar is the Chief Solutions Officer at Mphasis.
Artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) have captured the attention of businesses across industries for their ability to help in customer service, media, entertainment, retail, finance and healthcare, among other use cases and industries.
Gartner predicts that, by 2026, over 80% of enterprises will have used GenAI application programming interfaces (APIs) or models and/or implemented GenAI-enabled applications in production environments. In 2023, less than 5% of companies had done so. Bloomberg Intelligence, likewise, found that the GenAI market stood at $40 billion in 2022 but is expected to surge to $1.3 trillion over the next decade.
One of the key principles guiding my company's approach to the adoption of these technologies is the recognition that companies must make different considerations for each of the various use cases. Rather than succumbing to a one-size-fits-all mentality, organizations must conduct thorough assessments of their unique needs.
While GenAI may be the optimal solution for certain scenarios, others may be adequately addressed by more conventional approaches. Many tasks don't necessitate the sophisticated capabilities of an LLM.
For basic applications such as data analysis, classification or filtering, simpler and less computationally expensive solutions could be equally effective and more efficient. In other words, machine learning and classical AI solutions remain formidable contenders in the technology arsenal.
Using Specialized LLMs For Targeted Solutions
The emergence of specialized LLMs tailored for specific industries underscores the importance of targeted solutions.
Whether in healthcare, finance or other sectors, specialized LLMs highlight the importance of targeted solutions for industries. Designed with specific domain knowledge and terminologies in mind, these tailor-made models can offer significant advantages over generic LLMs. For instance:
• An LLM trained in medical reports can identify key findings and generate concise summaries, saving doctors and nurses valuable time in reviewing patient charts.
• An LLM trained in historical financial data can identify subtle patterns and anomalies that might indicate fraudulent activity, improving security and preventing financial losses.
• In the legal domain, a specialized LLM can identify potential issues and inconsistencies within complex contracts, reducing the risk of errors and omissions in contract reviewing.
Such specialized LLMs help improve efficiency, accuracy and decision-making. The question then arises: How do we effectively leverage these specialized LLMs?
Here, the options vary. Organizations may opt for in-house development, leveraging internal expertise to tailor solutions to their precise requirements. Alternatively, some vendors already offer solutions with a streamlined path to implementation. The choice ultimately hinges on factors, such as resource availability, strategic alignment and time-to-market. That said, ensuring that you have the necessary digital infrastructure for training these LLMs is crucial.
Navigating Productivity
GenAI and similar technologies can speed up productivity growth, which could help counterbalance a decline in job growth and foster overall economic expansion.
Projections by McKinsey suggest that automating specific tasks with these technologies could boost global productivity by 0.5% to 3.4% annually from 2023 to 2040, depending on how quickly automation is adopted. GenAI alone could contribute 0.1 to 0.6 percentage points to this growth.
Implementing a generative AI-based internal knowledge management system, where employees can respond to customer queries in real time can also help enhance efficiency, improve customer satisfaction and streamline communication processes.
From a business perspective, organizations must ensure employees are ready to harness AI quickly and efficiently. Organizations can help employees form groups and give them internal projects that have real-life implications, which would encourage them to train in AI. This would include learning how to effectively use products like CoPilot, Code Whisperer and others.
Collaborating For Enhanced Security
GenAI—which relies on vast datasets for its training—has raised significant privacy apprehensions. In particular, GenAI models' susceptibility to manipulation or exploitation underscores the urgency for preemptive risk evaluations and mitigation strategies.
Collaborating with internal or external cybersecurity specialists is indispensable for bolstering GenAI systems against potential threats from malefactors. Indeed, security emerges as a paramount concern, underscoring the necessity for robust partnerships and proactive measures to avert risks.
Navigating this complex landscape requires strategic investment as well as collaboration on targeted initiatives and understanding practical GenAI uses for an enterprise embarking on its adoption journey. As we move forward, collaborations will also be necessary to address ethical considerations and potential workforce impacts will also be crucial in ensuring AI's responsible and successful integration into the future of enterprise innovation.

title: AI Is Moving Biology From Science To Engineering, Advancing Medicine
text:
The marriage of data, new algorithms, and biology is leading to innovative engineering of biological processes and the development of new healthcare treatments and diagnostic products and services. At Nvidia’s GTC conference last month, Jensen Huang put it this way: “For the very first time in human history, biology has the opportunity to be engineering, not science.”
Leading the company at the center of the new AI infrastructure, Huang is intimately familiar with the burgeoning entrepreneurial and investment activity in the emerging field of digital biology and its implications for healthcare. “The future of medicine lies at the intersection of AI and biology,” Micha Breakstone, co-founder and CEO of Somite.ai told me recently. Allon Klein, another Somite.ai co-founder, called the process of turning a cell into a specific treatment for a specific ailment, “the most sophisticated therapy that has ever been invented,” highlighting the complex engineering challenge of taking a cell, step-by-step, through the process of development.
While Somite.ai is aiming to bring, within the next two years, its first therapeutic asset to phase-1 clinical trials, other startups are already demonstrating proven solutions, primarily with AI-driven diagnostic devices. For example, the FDA just granted the first ever clearance for a fully autonomous AI for portable diabetic retinopathy screening, developed by AEYE Health. 85% of patients with diabetes over the age of 40 could develop diabetic retinopathy, the leading cause of blindness in the working age population. Now they can benefit from an affordable early diagnostic screening solution, applied without dilation at a clinic, the pharmacy or even at home. There are approximately 40 million people with diabetes in the U.S. and over 500 million worldwide, all of whom are at risk of diabetic retinopathy, and early diagnosis and intervention are key for sight-loss prevention.
AEYE Health’s solution is one of 171 artificial intelligence and machine learning-enabled medical devices approved so far by the FDA. “Digital health technologies are playing an increasingly significant role in many facets of our health and daily lives, and AI/ML is powering important advancements in this field,” says the FDA.
Since 2012, the number of FDA-approved AI-related medical devices has increased by more than 45-fold, according to the 2024 AI Index. In 2022, the FDA approved 139 AI-related medical devices, a 12.1% increase from 2021, and the FDA expected that the number of approved AI/ML-enabled devices will grow 30+% year-over-year in 2023. A significant majority of approved devices were related to radiology.
These AI/ML-enabled medical devices, focused on narrow healthcare challenges, herald a new era of digital biology, where the very complex processes of life with its myriad elements can be engineered to yield robust and repeatable healthcare treatments and interventions. Aviv Regev, the co-recipient with Allon Klein of the 2021 James Prize in Science and Technology Integration, for “forging new ways to unite the disciplines of biology, computational science, and engineering,” explained in a recent interview why AI is so important to advancing biomedicine: “Many of the problems that we try to solve in biomedicine, [are] bigger than we would ever be able to perform experiments or collect data.”
AI is a great tool, said Regev, for search and discovery in “universes that appear extremely big… but in fact have a lot of structure and constraint in them.” When you apply AI to biology, “you can actually go after these problems that appear too big that are so important to understanding the causes of disease or devising the next drug.”
Joshua March and Kasia Gora, co-founders of SCiFi Foods, concur: “We are now at a critical inflection point in our ability to predict and engineer complex biological systems—transforming biology from a wet and messy science into an engineering discipline… it is clear that the combination of AI technology and advancements in automation with easy genetic editing means that we are already at the point where we can engineer biology to an extent never before possible.”
Investors also agree. The first quarter of 2024, says CB Insights, “was a brighter spot for the digital health market, which has struggled amid the broader venture slowdown. Digital health funding grew 48% quarter-over-quarter in Q1’24. This growth was supported by an increase in $100M+ mega-rounds, which were largely directed at biotech startups and other players leveraging AI.”

title: How ChatGPT Can Make Writing Easier — And What To Avoid
text:
The launch of ChatGPT 17 months ago is considered by many to be a technological inflection point as significant as the launch of the integrated circuit, the internet, and the iPhone. As with any such disruption, each novelty brings out legions of detractors and supporters.
To address both sides of the issue, let’s examine the positive aspects of ChatGPT and, as a cautionary tale, allay the concerns of the detractors.
Generating content
As soon as ChatGPT came out, students started using the technology to do their written assignments which led to charges of cheating as this article by Michael Nietzel indicates. Businesspeople, too, started using the technology to do their daily work—emails, reports, marketing communications, product/service descriptions—and while businesspeople are not likely to be charged with cheating, the practice does have the downside of coming across as either bland, generic, or flowery. The title and subtitle of an article in The Atlantic says it all: “ChatGPT is Dumber Than You Think: Treat it like a toy not a tool.”
Instead, set an honor code for yourself. Never use generative AI tools to generate content from scratch. First, do a rough draft of your own. Then turn to the bot as a productivity tool and prompt it for a draft. Use any ideas or phrases from the bot and work them into a second draft of your own. Be sure you keep both drafts separate to maintain the integrity of your honor code.
Editing content
Read that second draft, now focusing on the language. To heighten the accuracy and color of your description, query the bot again for synonymous words or idiomatic phrases. You can also use dictionary.com, thesaurus.com, or Google’s Power Thesaurus, but if you give ChatGPT a sense of what you’re looking for, its natural language can provide closer suggestions. Don’t just cherry-pick from the list; use your native intuition to make the choice that fits best.
Enriching content
As you develop your text, look for additional information that supports and adds depth to your ideas. If the information you find is lengthy or complex, copy and paste it into the bot and prompt it to simplify. Read the simplification and then work the information into your original draft using your own words.
During the process, be sure to double check the accuracy of your research. ChatGPT is often not only inaccurate but as this New York Times article reports, can provide misinformation.
Polishing content
Continue to review your text. Remember that one of the most frequently cited adages among professional writers is “Writing is rewriting.” With each review, you should be implementing a practice known as “Spaced Learning,” or walking away from your text. It’s a human technique that predates ChatGPT. For context, the opposite of Spaced Learning is cramming—need I say more?
In using ChatGPT and other generative AI tools this way, you will be implementing “error-driven learning,” a practice drawn from technology that enables and improves human thinking. In a recent Wall Street Journal article, Professor Charan Ranganath who runs the Dynamic Memory Lab at the Center for Neuroscience at the University of California, Davis, references the work of two cognitive psychologist in 1990 who noted that “neural network models of artificial intelligence learn through trial and error.” Professor Ranganath then ran an experiment in his lab that “used neural network models to simulate what happens in the hippocampus—a critical brain area for rapid learning.” His results found “that the human brain can learn and retain far more through trial and error.”
So go ahead and use ChatGPT to help you generate, edit, enrich, and polish your content, but be sure to keep your hand on the tiller by using an equal measure of your own human capabilities.
